summary:
Vichada stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

No Vichada-specific law, enforcement practice or incident finding for trans people appears in the sources assembled for this record. What they carry is national reporting that bears directly on frontier departments of this kind.

Armed groups in Caquetá department ran a "social cleansing" campaign documented in July 2024. Flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend of hers had been killed. The reporting describes trans women given a week to leave and displaced across departments, and records discrimination that limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. In Guajira department, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Killings also occur in ordinary urban settings and go unpunished. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín on 4 April 2025. The assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April; she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents but no one had been arrested even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was", and solidarity events were held in several cities.

The national toll recorded across the sources is 41 trans women killed in 2023, eight killed between February and April 2024, 13 trans people killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders recorded by the Attorney General's Office between January and May 2025. Earlier reporting cited in the same coverage notes killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper.
tangentialFactors:
The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025. He praised the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

The two departments with documented flyer campaigns, Caquetá and Guajira, are the closest evidence the record holds for the threat model facing a border department such as Vichada: armed actors publicly naming trans people as targets, issuing deadlines to leave, and displacing them across departmental lines. Vichada itself is not named in that reporting.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports a Vichada-specific statute, police practice, notary procedure, detention incident or act of violence against a trans person. Whether armed-group flyer or "social cleansing" campaigns of the Caquetá and Guajira type have been documented inside Vichada itself is unresolved in this record and is not asserted here.

The status of the comprehensive trans law after its 2025 legislative consideration is unresolved; no source states whether it was enacted.

The arrest position in the Sara Millerey case is stated as of the 14 April 2025 report, when no one had been detained. Later developments are not sourced.

The counts in the inventory are not reconciled because their denominators differ: 41 and 8 refer to trans women, 13 to trans people killed by hate, and 35 to LGBTI murders recorded over a different period. They are reported as separate figures rather than combined.

Whether the November 2025 "trans" and "non-binary" identification markers are issued in practice at Vichada's civil registry offices is not sourced.
